fixes.cite: Comisión Nacional sobre la Desaparición de Personas, Nunca Más, 20 September 1984 (Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture; US Institute of Peace truth commission digest; Wikipedia for the child figure)
fixes.victims_note: report: no fewer than 200 children under 15 kidnapped (figure via Wikipedia, citing the report); 8,960 disappearances recorded in all (Wikipedia gives 8,961)
fixes.d: The National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, created by President Raúl Alfonsín on 15 December 1983 and chaired by Ernesto Sábato, delivered its report Nunca Más on 20 September 1984. It recorded 8,960 forced disappearances between 1976 and 1983 and stated that no fewer than 200 children under 15 had been kidnapped; babies were taken with their parents or born to pregnant prisoners in detention camps and given to military families. The report was key evidence in the 1985 Trial of the Juntas.

note: Dates, chair and children findings confirmed (encyclopedia.com, USIP, Wikipedia). Count changed to 8,960 (USIP and encyclopedia; Wikipedia says 8,961); the unsourced 2012 'systematic plan' sentence was replaced with the 1985 trial fact. The '200 children' figure is only in Wikipedia; the Nunca Más text itself (desaparecidos.org) was blocked, so it is kept as url2.

fixes.cover: The network bribed a group of detectives for advance warning of police scrutiny; the Commission was highly critical of how police, prosecutors and public servants handled child sex-offence cases
fixes.d: The Royal Commission into the NSW Police Service under Justice James Wood (1994–1997) had its terms widened in 1995 to cover paedophile networks, the care of at-risk minors and police guidelines for investigating sex offences against minors; Volume IV of its final report is the paedophile inquiry. It found a network involving convicted offender Colin Fisk that shared child abuse material, procured under-age sexual partners and invested in an under-age male brothel in Surry Hills, and that it had a corrupt relationship with a group of detectives who sold it advance warning of police scrutiny. The Commission found no compelling evidence for claims of a large ring of prominent professionals protected by senior police.

note: Only Wikipedia found for this (it cites the report); all facts match it. Kept Wikipedia as url and say so; Wikipedia does not give Volume IV's date, so 1997 is from the Commission's end date. Wording on bribes softened to match.

fixes.d: The Family and Community Development Committee of the Parliament of Victoria tabled 'Betrayal of Trust', its report of the Inquiry into the Handling of Child Abuse by Religious and Other Non-Government Organisations, in November 2013. It found 'substantial criminal child abuse' over a long period by priests and members of religious orders in Victoria, and a culture in religious organisations that allowed systemic criminal abuse. Its recommendations would compel religious leaders to report child abuse to police and strip the Catholic Church of its virtual immunity from being sued.

note: Tablet (15 Nov 2013) and Guardian (12 Nov 2013) reposts on BishopAccountability support the findings and cover text; the exact 13 November tabling date is not in them, so d now says November 2013, and the recommendations sentence was reworded to what the Guardian states.

fixes.cite: Flemish expert panel on intercountry adoption (findings 2021, final report dated 15 February 2023); Vlaams Centrum voor Adoptie, Ethiopia investigation (Brussels Times, 23 November 2023); Belga News Agency
fixes.victims_note: 936 children adopted from Ethiopia to Flanders 1996–2017; investigations opened for 12 families
fixes.d: After reports of malpractice in adoptions from Ethiopia in 2019, the Flemish government appointed an independent expert panel on intercountry adoption, which delivered its findings in 2021 (final report dated 15 February 2023), and funded the Flemish Centre for Adoption to examine Ethiopian adoptions from 1997 to 2015. Preliminary conclusions found that the true story sometimes differed from the adoption files and that in the worst cases children had not been given up voluntarily by their birth parents. The panel's report led to screening of every country of origin, after which Flanders stopped adoptions from Vietnam and then from Gambia, Haiti and Morocco.

note: Brussels Times and the ACT database page support the Ethiopia and panel facts. Gambia, Haiti and Morocco were not in either source, so url2 now points to Belga News Agency, which reports those halts; the database page was dropped.

fixes.who: Users of the Orkut social network and offenders across Brazil; the CPI's hearings were credited with the fall of a Pará state deputy, Luiz Afonso Sefer, convicted at first instance in 2010
fixes.d: The Federal Senate's parliamentary inquiry into paedophilia, chaired by Senator Magno Malta, worked for almost three years, the longest CPI to date, and its rapporteur Demóstenes Torres handed a final report of nearly 1,700 pages to police and prosecutors in December 2010. It signed a conduct agreement with Google, the Federal Police and prosecutors to lift secrecy on Orkut pages linked to child sexual abuse. Rádio Senado reported that hundreds of people were arrested or indicted after its work, and Malta credited the CPI's hearings with the fall of Belém state deputy Luiz Afonso Sefer; Sefer was convicted in 2010 of raping a child, but the case has since been overturned, reinstated and annulled on appeal and, as of February 2026, his 20-year sentence had not been carried out. Laws passed during its work criminalised possession of child abuse material and ordered the closure of businesses where children were exploited.

note: Both Rádio Senado pages confirmed the length, report, Google/Orkut agreement, arrests and laws. The source did not say Sefer testified or was jailed: O Liberal (14 Feb 2026, oliberal.com/policia/sefer-esta-ha-16-anos-impume-e-em-liberdade-desde-a-primeira-sentenca-1.1084803) shows he has never been imprisoned and appeals are pending, so d and who were corrected.

fixes.d: Retired judge Fred Kaufman, asked by Nova Scotia's government in November 1999 to review its response, delivered 'Searching for Justice: An Independent Review of Nova Scotia's Response to Reports of Institutional Abuse' to Justice Minister Michael Baker on 31 January 2002. The province's compensation programme for people abused in provincial youth institutions, expected to draw about 300 claims, had received 1,264 by the time it closed in 2000 and paid about $39 million in compensation and counselling. Kaufman stated that sexual and physical abuse did occur, but found the programme 'seriously flawed', found significant evidence of false and exaggerated claims, and found that employees were branded as abusers without recourse. He made 105 recommendations.

note: NS government release confirms title, delivery date and November 1999 start; the Irish Times column confirms 1,264 claims, $39 million, the findings and 105 recommendations. The 'little validation' detail was not in either source and was removed.

fixes.who: Catholic clergy, religious and lay church workers; 152 priests, 10 bishops, 9 deacons, 15 lay people and 27 non-clerical members of orders among those investigated
fixes.d: Chile's National Prosecutor's Office reviewed sexual abuse by members of the Catholic Church nationally. Its balance of 30 April 2019 counted 166 investigations and 221 people investigated (152 priests, 10 bishops, 9 deacons, 15 lay people and 27 non-clerical members of orders), and 248 victims, of whom 131 were children or adolescents, 35 adults and 82 not recorded. In July 2018 the office had already reported five cases of alleged cover-up or obstruction aimed at bishops or superiors of congregations.

note: El Dínamo confirms all 2019 figures. The Scicluna-mission/raids framing and 'bishops mostly for cover-up' were not in the sources and were removed; the cover-up line now uses what Cooperativa (July 2018) states.

fixes.d: The BdP commissioned IPP Munich, working with the Dissens institute, to study sexualised violence in the association from its founding in 1976 to 2006. Presented on 29 February 2024, the study identified 103 victims (123 including cases that could not be dated or assigned) and 36 accused (50 with the same additions), almost all male; most incidents were in the 1980s and 1990s. It found two main perpetrator types, older adult leaders and adolescents or young adults who used leadership roles, and named weak oversight of young leaders, informal power imbalances, strong group loyalty and silence about sexuality as risk factors.

note: IPP press release confirms all figures, dates and findings; 'handling of rumours' was not in the release and was replaced by the risk factors it lists.

fixes.d: The German Conference of Catholic Religious Superiors (DOK) surveyed 392 orders and published the results on 26 August 2020. The 291 orders that answered, covering 88% of members, recorded accusations against at least 654 members and 58 other staff, from at least 1,412 children, adolescents or wards, about 80% of them male. Accusations were recorded in 53 of 77 male orders and 47 of 214 female orders. About 80% of the accused had died. The DOK said there were further unreported cases and that its survey was not a scientific study comparable to the bishops' 2018 study.

note: America/CNS confirms all figures. The claim that orders were 'left out of the 2018 MHG study' is not in the source (it says the survey cannot be compared with that study), so that sentence was replaced; 'in 2019' removed as the year of the survey is not stated.

fixes.cover: The report found that Archbishop Robert Zollitsch (from 2003) ignored canon law, did not report abuse suspicions to the Vatican although required from 2002, and that files were manipulated; Archbishop Oskar Saier (1978–2002) transferred offenders without informing parishes.
fixes.d: The archdiocese's independent reappraisal commission presented a roughly 600-page report on 18 April 2023, examining 24 cases in depth from 1945 onward. The commission chair, Magnus Striet, said more than 540 people were assumed to have been victims of more than 250 clerics; an earlier count had found at least 442 victims. It found that former archbishop Robert Zollitsch, who also chaired the German Bishops' Conference from 2008 to 2014, failed up to the point of deliberate concealment and ignored canon law, and that his predecessor Oskar Saier transferred offenders without informing parishes.

note: Vatican News confirms every figure and finding, including no reports to Rome from 2002 and manipulated files. Zollitsch's term end differs between sources (2013 vs 2014), so the cover text now says 'from 2003'.

fixes.cite: University of Osnabrück, interim report for the Diocese of Osnabrück, 20 September 2022 (The Pillar via BishopAccountability); The Tablet, 29 March 2023
fixes.cover: The interim report found Bishop Franz-Josef Bode, in the first decades of his term, repeatedly left accused priests in office and gave some roles, including leadership in youth ministry, that enabled further offences; Bode's resignation was accepted on 25 March 2023.
fixes.d: Researchers at the University of Osnabrück, commissioned by the diocese, presented a roughly 600-page interim report on 20 September 2022 on sexual violence against minors and vulnerable people by clergy since 1945; a final report was due in September 2024. The interim report found that Bishop Franz-Josef Bode (from 1995) repeatedly left accused priests in office, including some whose danger was hard to doubt, and assigned some to posts, including youth ministry, that enabled further abuse. Bode at first declined to resign, but after a canonical complaint by the German bishops' victims' advisory board he stepped down, citing his responsibility, and Pope Francis accepted his resignation on 25 March 2023.

note: The Pillar repost confirms the interim report facts. The second url (Dec 2022) says Bode had NOT resigned, so it was replaced with The Tablet (29 Mar 2023) for the resignation. The final report's 2024 publication was not confirmed (only 'expected September 2024'), and named authors were removed from cite.

fixes.d: Germany's federal Independent Commission for the Investigation of Child Sexual Abuse (UKASK) published a case study on sport on 27 September 2022, based on 72 reports from victims and witnesses and three personal accounts. Most abuse happened in organised club sport, especially competitive sport, by mostly male coaches, trainers or teachers in positions of power, and two-thirds of victims were abused repeatedly. Nearly a fifth of reports concerned sport in the GDR. Few cases had been uncovered or dealt with; victims often found their accounts denied, played down or covered up.

note: epd/evangelisch.de confirms every figure and finding; wording on disclosure adjusted to match ('denied, played down or covered up').

fixes.d: The Spanish Episcopal Conference hired the law firm Cremades & Calvo-Sotelo in February 2022 to audit sexual abuse in the Church. The church announced its findings on 21 December 2023: at least 2,056 minor victims and 1,383 complaints, without saying how many clergy were accused. The figure is far below the estimate of more than 200,000 victims since 1940 published in October 2023 by an independent commission appointed by parliament, and the bishops said it was 'obvious that the number is higher'.

note: The Local/AFP confirms hire date, announcement date, 2,056 and 1,383. The comparison body was corrected from 'the Ombudsman's survey' to what the source says (an independent commission appointed by parliament, October 2023, 200,000+ victims).

fixes.d: A French Senate joint information mission chaired by Catherine Deroche, with Marie Mercier and Michelle Meunier as rapporteurs, presented its conclusions on 29 May 2019 after hearing more than 60 people. Meunier described a 'systemic problem' in the Catholic Church, which the report put down to the sacred status of priests, the lack of checks on power, fear of scandal and a strong culture of secrecy; it flagged centres for disabled minors and sports federations as high-risk. It made 38 recommendations, including checking the sex-offender register (FIJAISV) before every hire to work with minors. A request by Socialist senators for a full commission of inquiry into the Church was refused by the law committee.

note: Public Sénat confirms all facts (headline says 38 recommendations, body says about forty). Report number 529 in cite was not checked against the PDF.

fixes.d: After Michael Gove's statement of 27 March 2014, 14 investigations were carried out by councils, institutions and successor organisations into information linking Jimmy Savile to their children's homes and schools in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s. The Department for Education statement of 26 February 2015 reported that none reached firm conclusions: many informants were judged credible, but there was not enough corroborating evidence for definite findings. Lucy Scott-Moncrieff's independent oversight found the investigations had been conducted in an appropriate and robust fashion.

note: GOV.UK statement confirms dates, the named organisations, the outcome and the oversight finding; minor rewording only.

fixes.cover: IICSA found a culture of cover-up and denial; very senior figures at the school or abbey were perpetrators and staff were warned to say nothing; Abbot Martin Shipperlee's handling of allegations showed serious shortcomings.
fixes.d: IICSA's report of 24 October 2019 found abuse at St Benedict's School over more than 30 years, in a 'sadistic and predatory' atmosphere where harsh physical punishment often led to sexual abuse. Since 2003 four staff connected to the school had been convicted of offences against more than 20 children, and the inquiry received at least 18 further allegations against them and eight other monks and teachers. It found serious shortcomings in Abbot Martin Shipperlee's handling of allegations; he resigned during the investigation, saying some of the failings were his.

note: IICSA news release confirms all facts; 'seriously deficient' was changed to the source's 'serious shortcomings'.

fixes.d: Frank Beck ran three Leicestershire council children's homes, The Poplars, Ratcliffe Road and The Beeches, between 1973 and 1986, and resigned in March 1986 after two male residential social workers complained of sexual advances. On 29 November 1991 he received five life sentences for assaults on more than 100 children; police took statements from nearly 400 children. The Leicestershire inquiry chaired by Andrew Kirkwood QC, reported in 1993, was strongly critical of the management of the county's social services, finding that early warnings were ignored, supervision was absent and complaints were poorly investigated. Its hearings were held in private.

note: Wikipedia and The Therapeutic Care Journal agree on homes, dates, verdict and Kirkwood's findings; the Independent (1994) copy was blocked, so Wikipedia stays as url. first_report removed because Kirkwood found earlier warnings had been ignored, so 1986 was not the first report.

fixes.d: After thousands of anonymous accounts were posted to the Everyone's Invited website, the government asked Ofsted to review sexual abuse in schools and colleges. Its report of 10 June 2021, based on visits to 32 state and private schools and colleges and talks with more than 900 young people, found sexual harassment had become normalised: 79% of girls said sexual assault of any kind happens 'a lot' or 'sometimes' between peers and 64% said so of unwanted touching. Many teachers underestimated the problem and pupils saw no point in reporting.

note: ITV News confirms all figures; percentages reworded to the survey's wording.

fixes.d: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's eleventh set of findings, published on 5 March 2024, covered boarding at Morrison's Academy from 1945 to 2007, when it stopped taking boarders. Lady Smith found children were abused, mainly physically and emotionally, with some sexual abuse, including by a few older pupils. Boarding houses could operate as separate 'fiefdoms' without adequate oversight by school management until the 1990s, and a strong culture of not reporting discouraged children from speaking up.

note: SCAI news page confirms all findings; date given as 5 March 2024 (the page header says 4 March, the text says Tuesday 5 March).

fixes.d: The independent review chaired by Martin Henry, commissioned by the Scottish FA, published its final report on 11 February 2021, having been held back from 2018 until related criminal proceedings ended. It examined non-recent abuse mainly from the 1970s to the early 1990s and found that adults with a sexual interest in children moved easily through Scottish football and kept their activities hidden, with flawed decisions that sometimes meant little or no action. 33 people gave personal accounts; the review urged clubs including Celtic, Rangers and Hibernian to apologise publicly, and the Scottish FA apologised.

note: Clyde 1 (Rayo) report confirms the period, findings, 33 accounts, clubs and delay; the Scottish FA page confirms date, chair and apology.

fixes.d: The first inquiry by the Children's Commissioner for Wales, Peter Clarke, published in 2004, concluded that drama teacher John Owen committed serious acts of sexual impropriety against pupils at Ysgol Gyfun Rhydfelen. Owen was charged in September 2001 after four former pupils went to police and was found dead in October 2001, before trial. The commissioner found that when sixth-formers complained in 1991 the Mid Glamorgan education officer made no child protection referral, and that the county's director of education obstructed a proper investigation and issued a misleading statement; Owen was allowed to resign without disciplinary action. It recommended independent school disciplinary tribunals for Wales and an independent children's counselling service.

note: Community Care confirms the 1991 failures, obstruction and recommendations; Wikipedia confirms the 2001 charges, death and the commissioner's finding. Neither gives the publication date, so yf 2004 is unconfirmed.

fixes.d: A Tynwald scrutiny committee (Social Affairs Policy Review Committee) chaired by David Cretney reported on 6 October 2018 on the 'horrific physical, emotional and sexual abuse' by Joseph Marshall while he ran Knottfield children's home with his wife between 1973 and 1983, and made 11 recommendations. Marshall had been convicted of 13 offences relating to Knottfield in 1992 and was jailed for six years in April 2022 for sexually abusing two boys there. The report was withdrawn during the criminal case; the Isle of Man Government apologised on 16 January 2023 for mistakes that contributed to the abuse and supported all 11 recommendations.

note: Manx Radio (6 Oct 2018) and the gov.im apology confirm all facts; 'the authorities had failed the children' was not in either source and was replaced with the government's own apology wording.

fixes.d: The Irish government asked senior counsel Roderick Murphy to inquire after former Olympic coach Derry O'Rourke was jailed for 12 years for abusing 11 girl swimmers. His 165-page report (1998) found that children had come to believe abuse was a normal part of their training, and a 'total systems failure' in the Irish Amateur Swimming Association. It noted Garda investigations into two other coaches and made more than 100 recommendations; the minister cut the association's funding.

note: Irish Echo (1998 article reposted) and Irish Times (18 June 1998) confirm the report, O'Rourke's sentence, findings and recommendations; the Irish Times names Gibney as one of the coaches whose cases the Leinster branch handled. 'Ineptitude' was not in the source and was removed.

fixes.d: The Government of Jamaica appointed a four-member review panel chaired by Sadie Keating in December 2002, after a public campaign about abuse in children's homes. Its report, reported by the Jamaica Observer on 15 July 2003, found that children in homes and places of safety had been sexually abused, including by care-giving staff, and that nine of the 15 homes visited could not recall a Child Services Division inspection in the past three years.

note: Jamaica Observer confirms the panel, findings and inspection figure; it does not state the exact release date, so 'made public in July 2003' was softened.

cite: NOU 2026:7 Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit (Granskingsutvalget for utenlandsadopsjoner), presented 22 June 2026; Statsforvalteren i Innlandet, 3 July 2026; summary for children published by the committee

fixes.cite: NOU 2026:7 Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit (Granskingsutvalget for utenlandsadopsjoner), presented 22 June 2026; Statsforvalteren i Innlandet, 3 July 2026; summary for children published by the committee
fixes.d: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.

note: The regjeringen.no news page did not load; the committee's children's summary (url2) confirms countries, 20,000+ adoptees and the examples, and Statsforvalteren confirms the 22 June date and main conclusion. The 20 June 2023 appointment date could not be confirmed, so d says 2023.

fixes.d: The independent commission 'Wyjaśnienie i Naprawa', set up in October 2024 and chaired by journalist Tomasz Krzyżak, presented its findings on 12 February 2026 after reviewing diocesan files from 1992 to January 2025. It found at least 50 children harmed, 96% of them under 15, and 29 people accused, 23 of them diocesan clergy; 19 of the 23 priests were confirmed offenders in church or state proceedings. Bishops were repeatedly alerted but in some cases took no action, and accused priests were often transferred rather than punished. The commission reported eight people to prosecutors.

note: Notes from Poland confirms all figures; the claim that it was the first such diocesan report in Poland is not in the source and was removed.

cite: Special Court for Sierra Leone, Prosecutor v. Charles Ghankay Taylor, trial judgment 26 April 2012 (JusticeInfo/Hirondelle; UN News; UN Office of the SRSG for Children and Armed Conflict)

fixes.cite: Special Court for Sierra Leone, Prosecutor v. Charles Ghankay Taylor, trial judgment 26 April 2012 (JusticeInfo/Hirondelle; UN News; UN Office of the SRSG for Children and Armed Conflict)
fixes.who: Charles Taylor, former President of Liberia; Revolutionary United Front (RUF) and allied rebel forces he aided
fixes.d: On 26 April 2012 the Special Court for Sierra Leone, sitting in The Hague, convicted former Liberian president Charles Taylor on all 11 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, on the basis of aiding and abetting crimes by the Revolutionary United Front during Sierra Leone's civil war, including sexual slavery and the recruitment and use of children under 15 as fighters. He was sentenced to 50 years in prison in May 2012.

note: JusticeInfo, UN News and the UN children-and-armed-conflict office confirm the conviction, counts, sexual slavery and child soldiers, and the 50-year sentence. The AFRC link and the appeal date were only in Wikipedia and were removed.

fixes.d: The Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation (CAVR) published its final report, Chega!, in 2005, covering 1974 to 1999. It found that at least 4,000 children were forcibly taken from their families and moved illegally to Indonesia during the occupation, by military units, some of which used them as child soldiers or servants, and by Islamic organisations that converted them; children were often renamed and lost contact with their families. It called separating a child from their true identity, culture, religion or language a grave breach of the Fourth Geneva Convention. CAVR and the joint Indonesia–Timor-Leste Commission of Truth and Friendship recommended a commission to search for the missing children, which was never created.

note: JusticeInfo confirms the 4,000 figure, perpetrators, Geneva Convention finding and the uncreated search commission; minor rewording. 'Renamed' is shown through a named case in the article rather than stated as a general finding.

fixes.place: Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUC) and other missions; report issued at UN Headquarters, New York
fixes.d: On 24 March 2005 the Secretary-General transmitted the report of his adviser Prince Zeid Ra'ad Zeid Al-Hussein on sexual exploitation and abuse in UN peacekeeping. Of 105 allegations recorded across missions in 2004, about 45% involved sex with persons under 18; in MONUC (DR Congo) 72 allegations were received between May and September 2004, and women interviewed described 'rape disguised as prostitution', with sex often costing about $1 to $3. OIOS considered 7 of the MONUC cases it examined fully substantiated and found convincing evidence in 2 more. The report recommended binding standards for all personnel, a professional investigative capacity, on-site courts martial and DNA paternity testing.

note: UN doc A/59/710 confirms every figure and recommendation. 'Girls described' changed to 'women interviewed' as the report says. ll moved from New York to a DRC centroid (llc) to match iso3 COD and where the findings are centred.

fixes.cover: The US Attorney said Texas state agencies and the Texas Rangers had substantiated sexual abuse allegations at these facilities as early as the 2000s and that the problem persisted

note: DOJ press release of 1 August 2024 confirms the five facilities and all findings; cover reworded to attribute the statement to US Attorney Alamdar Hamdani's wording.

fixes.d: Stanley Patrick Weber, an Indian Health Service pediatrician, was convicted of sexually abusing young boys at IHS hospitals in Montana and South Dakota. A White House task force chaired by US Attorney Trent Shores released a report on 23 July 2020 finding that officials across the agency did not understand their legal duties to report suspected abuse, that the agency sometimes overlooked doctors' troubled work histories to fill posts, and that parts of its child-protection policy conflicted with federal law. After complaints, the agency had moved Weber to another IHS hospital, where he practised for another 21 years.

note: PBS Frontline confirms all facts; minor rewording.

fixes.d: On 30 September 2026 Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell released a report finding that more than 270 Catholic clergy abused nearly 1,000 children in the Dioceses of Worcester, Fall River and Springfield, with abuse dating back to the 1950s. She called it the first full public accounting of the abuse, misconduct and institutional failures in those dioceses. The report recommended proper investigation of allegations and transparent, accurate records, and Campbell called on Worcester, the only one of the three without a public list of credibly accused priests, to publish one.

note: WBUR confirms all figures. The link to a 2003 Boston report was not in the source and was removed.

cite: New York Attorney General, press release on agreement with the Diocese of Brooklyn, 16 April 2024; Insurance Journal / AP

fixes.cite: New York Attorney General, press release on agreement with the Diocese of Brooklyn, 16 April 2024; Insurance Journal / AP
fixes.cover: The diocese did not consistently follow its own procedures, sometimes did not disclose credible allegations and did not adequately monitor accused clergy; a priest who admitted abusing minors was defrocked in 2007 on condition of confidentiality and this was kept secret until 2017; another priest was moved between parishes after complaints
fixes.d: On 16 April 2024 the New York Attorney General announced an agreement after finding that the Diocese of Brooklyn had not consistently followed its own procedures for abuse complaints, applied inconsistent standards of proof and did not adequately monitor credibly accused clergy. In one case a priest who admitted repeatedly abusing minors was removed from duties without parishioners being told, and his 2007 defrocking was kept confidential until 2017; in another a priest was transferred between parishes after earlier concerns and went largely unmonitored despite a 2006 complaint. The diocese accepted new procedures, referral of all complaints to law enforcement and an independent secular monitor for at least three years.

note: Switched url to the NY AG's own press release, which confirms the date and findings; details corrected to match it (2007 defrocking kept secret until 2017; the second priest's complaints were not 'from the 1990s onward' in the AG text).

fixes.cite: Report of the Grand Jury, Philadelphia, released February 2011, as reported by CBS News, March 2011
fixes.d: A second Philadelphia grand jury reported in February 2011 that as many as 37 priests remained in active ministry despite credible allegations of sexual abuse. Two priests, a former priest and a Catholic school teacher were charged with raping boys, and Monsignor William Lynn, a former senior archdiocesan official, was charged and accused of transferring problem priests to new parishes without warning anyone of earlier complaints. On 8 March 2011 the archdiocese suspended 21 priests while their cases were reviewed.

note: CBS News confirms the 37 priests, the charges, Lynn's role and the 21 suspensions (8 March 2011). The exact report dates in cite (21 Jan / 10 Feb) and 'two-year investigation' were not in the source and were removed.

fixes.d: A Suffolk County grand jury report of about 180 pages, presented by District Attorney Thomas Spota in February 2003 after a nine-month investigation, found that at least 58 abusive priests had been protected by the Diocese of Rockville Centre. Officials used sham policies, a bogus 'intervention team' that silenced victims and a 'legal affairs' team that worked to block claims, moved abusers between parishes where they often had access to children, and disregarded advice to give them psychiatric care. The grand jury said the failures could not be attributed to incompetence.

note: Irish Times (13 Feb 2003) confirms all facts and the 43-priest secret archives. The statute-of-limitations sentence was not in the source and was removed.

fixes.cover: The Attorney General blamed police and prosecutors for not investigating allegations when they were first made; the Sisters of Providence had not produced documents the task force requested by the time the report was finished

note: Vermont AG release confirms dates, members, BuzzFeed trigger, ~300 pages, 1854–1974, no murder evidence and no charges; WCAX confirms 'it is clear abuse happened', the sexual abuse accounts, Donovan's criticism of police and prosecutors and the missing Sisters of Providence documents. Cover lightly reworded.

fixes.d: After a 14-year-old girl died in childbirth at a Johanne Marange Apostolic Sect shrine in August 2021, the Zimbabwe Gender Commission opened a public investigation on 24 September 2021 into sexual exploitation and abuse of girls and child marriages in apostolic sects. It identified compulsory virginity testing, wife pledging, betrothal and forced marriage in the Marange sect, and an earlier 2020 probe of branches around Marondera found girls of about 10 to 15 taken in as 'wives-in-waiting' and married at puberty. Its report for 2022 said it had received and investigated over 500 cases of child marriage and sexual exploitation and called for legislation regulating faith-based organisations.
fixes.cite: Zimbabwe Gender Commission investigation into apostolic sects (call for submissions 24 September 2021), as reported by The Herald (Zimbabwe), 2021; ZGC 2022 report as reported by CITE, 15 June 2023

note: The Herald and CITE confirm the facts. The Herald gives 24 September without a year (2021 inferred from context), and no General Notice number; the 500 cases are not limited to sects, as victims_note already says. Removed the unconfirmed General Notice number from cite.
